briefing.question: What does an election actually mean? Is a midterm a mandate, a check, or simply many local choices, and how should the losing side and the winning side read the people's will?
briefing.agreed: A count shows strength, not a mandate on everything.
briefing.split: Madison, a deliberate check; Burke, no flattery; Mill, strength not reasons; Polybius, correction; Rousseau, sum not will.

briefing.question: Who has the right to take a nation to war, and when does force used in self-defense become war in all but name?
briefing.agreed: Defend forces under attack; going further needs authority.
briefing.split: Aquinas, proportion; Hamilton, no campaign alone; Madison, Congress; Grotius, attack versus threat; Kant, ask who pays.

briefing.question: Who guards the guardians? How does a free people make sure votes are counted honestly without letting the counter's watchers become a threat to the vote itself?
briefing.agreed: Count honestly, and watch the watchers by known rules.
briefing.split: Plato, gentle to all; Madison, many overseers; Hamilton, via Congress; Blackstone, keep power away; Locke, losers must trust.

briefing.question: Can a majority vote settle what a person is, or what marriage is? Are some questions of right and wrong beyond the reach of popular sovereignty?
briefing.agreed: Votes do not make right; both sides appeal past majorities.
briefing.split: Douglas, each state; Lincoln, no right to do wrong; Tocqueville, justice limits; Aquinas, natural law; Mill, harm.

briefing.question: Can a nation inherit guilt, or only responsibility? What do the living owe for wrongs done by the dead?
briefing.agreed: No one alive is guilty; a nation can still be responsible.
briefing.split: Jaspers, political liability; Burke, debts with glories; Douglass, repentance; Aquinas, restore; Aristotle, distribution.

briefing.question: What is education for, forming the mind through struggle or equipping it with the best tools, and who has authority over what children learn?
briefing.agreed: Learning needs effort; those who answer for children decide.
briefing.split: Plato, still thinking; Aristotle, community; Newman, form first; Mill, no uniformity; Leo XIII, parents; Brandeis, size.

briefing.question: Can the gospel be claimed by a party, or does it judge every party? What does faithful Christian witness in politics look like?
briefing.agreed: No party owns the gospel; Christians may serve as citizens.
briefing.split: Augustine, two cities; Rauschenbusch, social demands; Machen, not a program; Williams, guard the church; King, thermostat.

briefing.question: How do we name evil truthfully, and what do Christians and nations owe to suffering strangers far away?
briefing.agreed: Victims are neighbours of any faith; names must follow facts.
briefing.split: Augustine, near bonds; Confucius, true names; Grotius, help without pretext; Hobbes, Nigeria first; Kant, aid not force.

briefing.question: When a nation's institutions are in crisis, is the Church's role to reconcile or to judge?
briefing.agreed: The Church is no party's chaplain; it prays for all.
briefing.split: Ambrose, plain crimes; Leo XIII, above party; Calvin, correct; John Paul II, democrats differ; Tocqueville, keep a voice.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first because the report names Federalist 51, and because he designed the two-year House term precisely so that frequent elections would keep one chamber close to the people. Burke is named for his Speech to the Electors of Bristol, the classic statement that a representative owes his voters his judgment, not only his obedience. Mill wrote a whole book on representative government, including a chapter on whether members should be bound by pledges and a defence of elections as a periodic muster of national opinion. Polybius is named for the mixed constitution, in which each power is checked by the others. Rousseau gives the sharpest objection: that a people who only vote are free only on election day. Tocqueville, who wrote on the omnipotence of the majority, sits at the cultural table tonight and is left off here. The candidates, the parties and the pollsters are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what an election means. Is a midterm a mandate, a check, or simply many local choices, and how should the winners and the losers read the people's will? The report gives one side as Democrats and their allies, who read the early calls as a verdict on the President, on the Iran conflict and fuel prices, on tariffs and affordability, and as a demand for a check on government by emergency and executive action. chairs.name: James Madison

turn.text: I designed a House that faces the voters every second year, and I gave the reason plainly. “Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectually secured.” (Federalist No. 52) A midterm is not an accident of the calendar; it is the machinery working as intended. Whatever else it is, it is the people's regular chance to say whether the government still shares their interests.

turn.text: But I never thought the vote alone was enough. “A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.” (Federalist No. 51) One of those precautions is the very thing the report's first side hopes for: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” (Federalist No. 51) If the voters divide power between the parties, that is not a failure to choose; it may be a choice to have each branch watch the other. If they hand both chambers to the president's party, they have chosen that too. Neither result is a blank cheque, because no result in my system ever is.

chairs.name: Polybius
chairs.tradition: Greek historian of the Roman constitution

turn.text: Mill measures opinion; I measured constitutions over centuries, and I saw them decay. “This is the regular cycle of constitutional revolutions, and the natural order in which constitutions change, are transformed, and return again to their original stage.” (Histories, Book VI, ch. 9) Kingship sinks into tyranny, aristocracy into oligarchy, democracy into the rule of violence. What slowed that wheel at Rome was a mixed constitution, in which consuls, senate and people each held real power.

turn.text: The cure was not that any one part won. “For when any one of the three classes becomes puffed up, and manifests an inclination to be contentious and unduly encroaching, the mutual interdependency of all the three, and the possibility of the pretensions of any one being checked and thwarted by the others, must plainly check this tendency” (Histories, Book VI, ch. 18) I would tell the first side that this is the old case for a check, and it is a sound one. I would tell the second side that the same logic protects them: if one party sweeps everything and grows puffed up, the next election is the instrument by which it is checked in turn. The point of the correction is balance, not the triumph of one class over another.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: can a nation inherit guilt, or only responsibility? What do the living owe for wrongs done by the dead? Scripture gives both strands. Ezekiel says “The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezekiel 18:20), while Daniel prays for his people, “We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly” (Daniel 9:5), and Nehemiah confesses that “both I and my father's house have sinned.” (Nehemiah 1:6) The report gives one side as Caribbean leaders and campaigners, who say slavery's harms still shape their nations' poverty and debt, that sorrow without apology is incomplete, and that repair begins with acknowledgment. The other side is opponents of apology and reparations, who say no one alive committed or suffered the crime, that Britain paid dearly to suppress the trade after 1807, that slavery existed across nearly every civilization, and that taxpayers' money is owed to present needs at home. We decide nothing tonight about any claim for money. Professor Jaspers, you begin.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what is education for, forming the mind through struggle or equipping it with the best tools, and who has authority over what children learn? The report gives one side as Google and advocates of AI in education, who say AI is now as basic as search itself, that students need to learn to use it well rather than be shielded from it, and that guided tools designed for learning are better than unfiltered chatbots at home.
